alt: Two equally weighted sections of 25 marks. Section A, Beliefs and Teachings, rewards belief, evidence and significance. Section B, Practices, rewards connecting belief to specific daily practice. In each, short questions build to a 12-mark response on a set passage; the paper lasts 1 hour 30 minutes for 50 marks.
caption: Two equal sections: revise beliefs and practices evenly.

alt: A table of the Five Pillars with their practice, conditions and significance: salah has prescribed times and needs wudu; zakat applies only above the nisab; sawm exempts the ill, travelling, pregnant, nursing and elderly; hajj is only for those physically and financially able.
caption: Conditions and significance are where marks are won or lost.

alt: Six rites in order: ihram, tawaf (seven circuits of the Ka'bah), sa'i between Safa and Marwah, standing at Arafat (highlighted as the essential rite), stoning the pillars at Mina and the sacrifice. Below, the chain of meaning: identical white garments make wealth and status invisible, so all stand equal before God.
caption: Name the rites, then explain the equality the white garments symbolise.

alt: Tawhid, the oneness of God, branches into three practical consequences: worship directed to God alone, no intermediaries, and the equality of all believers. Below, its opposite, shirk, is marked as the gravest sin.
caption: Tawhid is a belief with practical consequences for worship and equality.

alt: A schematic arc of the sun's path marks the five prayers: Fajr at dawn, Zuhr at midday, Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib at sunset and Isha at night. Cards add facing the Qiblah, rak'ahs and wudu, and contrast Salah with du'a and private prayer with Jummah.
caption: Five prescribed times from dawn to night, all facing the Qiblah.

alt: Eid-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, with zakat-ul-fitr given before the prayer. Eid-ul-Adha falls during Hajj, commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son, and its qurbani meat is shared in three parts: family, relatives and the poor.
caption: Fitr ends Ramadan; Adha falls during Hajj and recalls Ibrahim.

alt: A worked answer in three layers. For the individual, zakat purifies wealth and treats it as a trust from God. For the community, it redistributes to the poor, orphans, travellers and the indebted, reduces inequality and strengthens mutual responsibility. The key point: it is obligatory worship, unlike voluntary sadaqah.
caption: Individual, community, then the zakat–sadaqah distinction.
